fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. David asks, "Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). He doesn't dress it up first. I think it took real nerve to say that straight to the LORD.

Rain would be a fine thing to ask about, friend, but David never brings up the weather. After "How long, O LORD?" he asks, "Will You forget me forever?" That question is about being remembered, not about the forecast. David has his mind on something much closer than a cloud.

I'd love a bigger bakery myself, baker, but money never comes up in this psalm. David asks, "Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). He wants the LORD's attention, not a fatter wallet. Nothing in his question has a price tag on it.

His enemy, baker. David asks, "How long will my enemy dominate me?" (Psalm 13:2). The psalm never says who this enemy is. The enemy shows up again in verse 4, so I think he's weighing on David's mind.

A brother is a fair guess, friend, but this psalm doesn't name one. David says it's his enemy who dominates him (Psalm 13:2). The psalm doesn't name that enemy, so I won't make up a name either. Brothers will have to wait for another passage.

A servant doing the dominating would be a wild twist, like the dough bossing the baker around. But David never mentions a servant here. He asks, "How long will my enemy dominate me?" (Psalm 13:2). The enemy is the one on his mind.
Not quite, baker. David doesn't say his foes will mourn. He says, "and my foes rejoice when I fall." (Psalm 13:4). I think that's the part that stings.

A sword and spear is a fair guess, friend, but he never mentions a weapon in this psalm. He says, "But I have trusted in Your loving devotion…" (Psalm 13:5). Even with an enemy in the picture, his trust goes to the LORD, not to his gear.

A rejoicing house would be quite the sight, baker, with the walls doing a little dance. But David says, "my heart will rejoice in Your salvation." (Psalm 13:5). The one rejoicing is his heart. Houses can stay quiet.

I can see why you'd guess that, baker, but the psalm doesn't say his sorrow lifted. David gives this reason: "I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me." (Psalm 13:6). His song rests on the LORD's goodness.
